overview.body:
**Nwt** ​(*nut*) — ‌The Sky, ‌the Stars, ​the ​Vault of ​Night · ​Water-pot, ​sky — ‌belongs to ​the Egyptian ​tradition, ‌where it ​is catalogued ‌under the ​domain ‌"Sky, Stars, ​Cosmos". The ​name ​means "Water-pot, ​sky (Egyptian ​nwt)"[^1].

**Nwt** ‌is ​the sky ‌— not ​a metaphor ‌for ​it. Her ‌body is ​the ‌vault, starred ​across its ​length; her ‌lips ‌and womb ‌the gates ​through which ​the ‌sun passes ​at dusk ​and ‌dawn. Each ​night she ​swallows the ‌sun; ​each morning ‌she gives ​birth to ​it ​again, the ​great cosmic ‌rhythm ‌painted on ​temple ceilings ‌from Luxor ​to ​Dendera.[^2]

PuniCodex ‌restores the ‌name as ‌**Nwt** ‌and serves ​its temple ‌at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/nut/). ​The restoration ​aSCII-equivalent form ‌— ​a description ​computed from ​the displayed ‌form ​itself. The ​plain ASCII ​form ‌*nut* survives ​as a ‌modern convenience ​imposed ‌by the ​early domain-name ‌system; the ‌restoration, ​not the ​fallback, is ​the ​form the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

domains.body:
**Nwt** ​is the ‌sky — ‌not ​a metaphor ​for ​it. Her ​body is ​the ‌vault, starred ​across ​its length; ‌her lips ​and ‌womb the ​gates through ‌which ​the sun ​passes ​at dusk ​and dawn. ​Each ‌night she ​swallows ‌the sun; ​each morning ‌she ​gives birth ‌to ​it again, ‌the great ​cosmic ​rhythm painted ‌on temple ‌ceilings ‌from Luxor ​to ​Dendera.[^1]

### The ‌Starry Vault

​Her ​body is ‌painted ​blue across ​temple ceilings, ‌scattered ​with the ‌decans and ​planets ​she carries.

### ​Mother ​of the ‌Gods

By ‌Geb ​she bore ‌Osiris, ​Isis, Seth, ​Nephthys, and ‌Horus ‌the Elder ‌— the ‌third ​generation of ‌the ​Ennead.

### Swallower ​of the ​Sun

‌Each dusk ​the ​sun enters ​her mouth; ‌each ​dawn she ​births ​it — ‌time itself ​is ‌her digestion.

### ​Lady of ‌the ​Sycamore

She ‌appears ‌in tree-form ​pouring water ​and ​bread on ​the ‌dead from ‌a celestial ​sycamore.

symbols.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated with ‌Nwt ​concentrates ​in ​a ​small set ​of ‌recurring ​attributes, ​each ‌a compressed ​statement ‌about ​the ‌name:[^1]

- ​**The Starry ​Vault** ​— ​Her ​body ‌is painted ​blue ‌across ​temple ‌ceilings, ​scattered with ‌the ​decans ‌and ​planets ​she carries.
- ‌**Mother ‌of ‌the ​Gods** ​— By ‌Geb ​she ​bore ‌Osiris, ​Isis, Seth, ​Nephthys, ‌and ​Horus ‌the Elder ​— ​the ​third ​generation ‌of the ‌Ennead.
- ​**Swallower ‌of ​the ​Sun** — ‌Each ‌dusk ‌the ‌sun ​enters her ‌mouth; ​each ​dawn ​she ‌births it ​— ​time ​itself ‌is ​her digestion.
- ​**Lady ​of ‌the ​Sycamore** ‌— She ​appears ‌in ​tree-form ‌pouring ‌water and ​bread ​on ​the ​dead ‌from a ‌celestial ​sycamore.

sources.citation: Pyramid Texts (Nut as mother of the gods).

mythology.body:
Nut enters ​myth chiefly as the ‌forbidden wife: the sky ‌and the earth, ​she and Geb, were ​locked in an ​embrace Shu had to ​tear apart to create ​the world’s space. ‌Separated, she spends eternity ​arched over him, swallowing ​the sun he ‌receives back each dawn ​— the most ‌elegant creation image Egypt ​produced.[^1]

### The Embrace of ‌Geb and Nut ​(Heliopolitan Cosmogony)

Shu and ​Tefnut, the first air ​and moisture, bore ​Geb the earth and ​Nut the sky ‌— who loved so ​closely that no light ‌or creature could ​pass between them. On ‌Ra’s command, or by ​Shu’s own strength ‌in the tellings, the ​air god forced ‌them apart and holds ​them apart to this ​day: the atmosphere ‌itself is the wedge ‌of creation.[^2]

### The Birth ‌Bricks of the ​Gods (Pyramid Texts)

The ​old utterances make ‌Nut the great mother ​repeatedly: she who bore ​the gods on ‌her five epagomenal days ​— the days added ​outside the 360-day ‌year, won for her ​from the moon ‌in the game of ​senet. Osiris, Horus, Seth, ​Isis and Nephthys ​were born on those ​five days, the only ‌time the sky ‌goddess could labour.

### She ​Who Gives Birth ‌and Does Not Tire ​(Book of the Dead, ​spell 17)

Spell ‌17 invokes Nut as ‌the sow who eats ‌her piglets and ‌the mother who daily ​bears the sun: ‌‘I am Nut, the ​great one who gives ​birth to the ​gods.’ The deceased appeals ‌to her body as ​the ladder of ​ascent — to be ​‘a star imperishable’ ‌among her children was ​the standard hope of ​the afterlife.

### The ​Night Barque Within Her ‌(Solar Theology)

In the ​solar books the ‌sun god’s night journey ​runs through Nut’s ‌interior from mouth to ​womb; her body is ‌the Duat’s architecture. ‌New Kingdom royal tombs ​— from Thutmose III ​to Ramesses VI ​— paint her figure ​along the sarcophagus ‌hall so that the ‌king ascends through the ​goddess herself.

hieroglyphic-evidence.body:
The name Nwt is written in Egyptian hieroglyphs as a theonym with the divine determinative. Scribes used logographic and phonetic signs to represent the sounds and semantic class of the deity.

The restoration Nwt transliterates Egyptological convention, preserving the distinction between sign function and phonetic value.[^1]

sources.citation: Pyramid Texts (Nut as mother of the gods).

pyramid-texts.body:
The Pyramid Texts, inscribed in royal tombs of the Old Kingdom, contain the earliest references to Nwt. These spells map the king's journey through the afterlife and the divine forces that assist or oppose him.

The restored name Nwt reflects scholarly transliteration of those hieroglyphic spells.[^1]

sources.citation: Pyramid Texts (Nut as mother of the gods).

coffin-texts.body:
The Coffin Texts democratize the afterlife knowledge of the Pyramid Texts, inscribing spells on private coffins of the Middle Kingdom. Nwt appears in mortuary and cosmological passages that protect the deceased.

The Unicode restoration Nwt continues the Egyptological reading of those texts.[^1]

sources.citation: Pyramid Texts (Nut as mother of the gods).

book-of-the-dead.body:
The Book of the Dead, a New Kingdom compilation of spells, includes references and imagery connected with Nwt. Papyri and tomb vignettes present the deity in the landscape of judgment and transformation.

The restored spelling Nwt preserves the scholarly form used in modern editions.[^1]

sources.citation: Pyramid Texts (Nut as mother of the gods).
